Do GEO Gains Survive the Live Web? Evaluating In-the-Wild Visibility Gains of Generative Engine Optimization via LIVE-GEO

CCS: Information systems Evaluation of retrieval resultsCCS: Information systems Test collections
Runze Kong Affiliation: Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Ann Arbor, USA , Haibo Jin Affiliation: School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, USA , Xucheng Yu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, USA , Xiaoqi Wang Affiliation: [ , Huimin Zeng Affiliation: School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, USA and Haohan Wang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, USA email: haohanw@illinois.edu

Abstract.

Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content so that LLM-based search systems, also termed generative engines (GEs), rank it higher in their answers and recommendations. However, existing GEO evaluations typically rely on directly supplied text or controlled retrieval pipelines, and whether GEO gains survive the live Web remains unclear, leaving a gap in understanding how GEO strategies affect the visibility of live webpages when accessed and ranked by GEs. To address this gap, we introduce LIVE-GEO, a benchmark for Live, In-the-wild Visibility Evaluation for GEO. LIVE-GEO publishes GEO-rewritten products as live webpages. We use LIVE-GEO to evaluate five existing GEO strategies (CORE, C-SEO, E-GEO, AgenticGEO, and Statistics Addition), applying them to the product descriptions and reviews of 80 fictional brands across 18 product families. We run experiments on three GEs (ChatGPT with GPT-6, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, and Grok in Expert mode), four direct-text API evaluators (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Kimi, and Claude), and a direct-text local evaluator (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct). With frozen ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices, most direct-text evaluators and GEs receiving product URLs give CORE the highest Top-1 rate, reaching 66.3%–76.3% on the GEs, yet other strategies vary in relative performance, and the GEs select the same top product for only 48.8%–66.3% of brands. We also find that ChatGPT is sensitive to the order of candidate URLs: CORE’s Top-1 rate is 73.8% and 93.8% under two opposite fixed orders, and the randomized order used by LIVE-GEO yields 82.5%, between the two. In the numerical-faithfulness check, the JEV verifier agrees with the reference labels on 90.7% of 194 numerical benchmark cases and with human judgments on all 50 sampled descriptions, and it flags 86 of the 400 rewritten descriptions, including all 80 Statistics Addition descriptions.

Keywords: 
generative engine optimization, generative search, web visibility, benchmark

1. Introduction

Generative engine optimization (GEO) aims to enhance the visibility of web content in responses generated by large language model (LLM)-based search systems, also called generative engines (GEs) (Aggarwal et al., 2024). GEs combine web retrieval with an LLM that synthesizes responses from retrieved content (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Lewis et al., 2020; Nakano et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023b).

Prior GEO strategies have mainly been evaluated either by supplying text directly to an LLM or through controlled retrieval pipelines built by researchers. For example, GEO-Bench, C-SEO Bench, and E-GEO place the rewritten content in the LLM input together with a fixed set of competing sources and measure its visibility or rank in the generated response (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Puerto et al., 2025; Bagga et al., 2026). Because the candidate set is fixed in advance, these benchmarks evaluate selection but not retrieval. Other benchmarks also simulate the retrieval stage. For instance, SAGEO Arena and Counter-GEO-Bench build their own retrieval, reranking, and generation stages over collected web documents, so rewritten content is also evaluated at retrieval (Kim et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). Both settings are reproducible and easy to use, which supports controlled comparisons between GEO strategies. However, neither setting evaluates rewritten pages published on the live Web, even when it simulates the retrieval stage. In contrast, GEs retrieve and select web content through black-box pipelines (Aggarwal et al., 2024), and different GEs draw on different sources (Kirsten et al., 2026). GEO gains measured in controlled settings may therefore not transfer to GEs, and whether these gains survive when GEs access the rewritten pages on the live Web remains unclear.

To address this gap, we introduce LIVE-GEO (Live, In-the-wild Visibility Evaluation for GEO), a benchmark that publishes GEO-rewritten products on the live Web and observes how GEs rank them. LIVE-GEO covers 80 fictional brands across 18 product families. It runs as the public product site of a startup partner, so its pages are reachable by GEs in the same way as other commercial sites. The products of a brand share the same specifications and differ only in their descriptions, reviews, and a small price offset: an Original product generated from templates and rewritten products, each produced by one GEO strategy, so differences in a GE’s ranking of them come from the rewritten text rather than from the product itself. Users download the Original descriptions and reviews, rewrite them with their own GEO strategy, and upload the result. After our safety screening and numerical-faithfulness verification, the submission is published on our website as a new rewritten product, and users can then obtain its ranking from GEs.

We use LIVE-GEO to evaluate five existing GEO strategies, implemented from their released prompts or code. Specifically, we investigate four research questions (RQs) on LIVE-GEO: RQ1: How consistent is GEO visibility across GEs and direct-text evaluators? RQ2: How sensitive is visibility to repeated evaluation, candidate order, and public identity? RQ3: How do small price differences and URL entry conditions affect observed visibility? RQ4: How reliable are numerical-faithfulness flags, and how does applying them affect visibility? We answer all four in Section 4.2.

We compare three GEs used through their web interfaces, ChatGPT (GPT-6), Gemini (3.6 Thinking), and Grok (Expert mode), with five direct-text evaluators: four API models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.6, and Claude Sonnet 5.5) and a local model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct). With frozen ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices and product URLs supplied to the GEs, CORE achieves the highest Top-1 rate with seven of the eight evaluators, including rates of 66.3%–76.3% on the GEs, yet the GEs agree on the top product for only 48.8%–66.3% of brands, and agreement between direct-text evaluators and GEs ranges from Spearman ρ=0.50\rho=0.50 to ρ=−0.31\rho=-0.31. CORE’s Top-1 rate on ChatGPT ranges from 73.8% to 93.8% across opposite fixed orders and differs between the unmasked repeat (83.8%) and masked run (76.3%), whereas a repeat with the same presentation is stable (ρ=0.85\rho=0.85), and price or URL-entry changes affect the values but not the Top-1 leader. The numerical-faithfulness verifier agrees with the reference labels on 90.7% of 194 benchmark cases and with the human majority on all 50 reviewed descriptions.

2. Related Work

GEO Content Optimization Strategies. Heuristic GEO strategies rely on manually designed rules or criteria to guide content rewriting. Statistics Addition incorporates quantitative statistics into the content, while Cite Sources adds relevant source citations (Aggarwal et al., 2024). The Content Improvement strategy of C-SEO Bench (C-SEO in this paper) combines multiple such transformations into a single rewriting strategy (Puerto et al., 2025). By contrast, feedback-based GEO strategies derive optimization signals from GE responses. AutoGEO learns GE preferences from how documents are used in generated responses and applies these preferences to prompt-based rewriting and reinforcement learning (Wu et al., 2026). AgenticGEO further approximates such preference feedback with a surrogate critic and combines it with self-evolving strategy search (Yuan et al., 2026). E-GEO iteratively optimizes rewriting prompts to improve product rankings (Bagga et al., 2026). Strategic text sequences (STS) and StealthRank study ranking-oriented adversarial optimization (Kumar and Lakkaraju, 2024; Tang et al., 2026). CORE’s query-based optimization revises appended content according to differences between observed and target rankings (Jin et al., 2026).

Evaluation Settings for GEO. GEO-Bench, C-SEO Bench, and E-GEO compare rewrites within preselected candidate sets, measuring visibility, citations, or rank once the candidates are fixed (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Puerto et al., 2025; Bagga et al., 2026). As in fixed-data IR benchmarks such as MS MARCO and BEIR, shared queries and sources support controlled comparisons (Nguyen et al., 2016; Thakur et al., 2021). Counter-GEO-Bench retrieves and reranks within five preselected sources per query to assess defenses against distorting rewrites (Zheng et al., 2026). SAGEO Arena reindexes rewrites in a crawled corpus and tracks visibility through retrieval, reranking, and generation, revealing that generation-stage gains can be lost upstream (Kim et al., 2026). Work on live GEs is of three kinds: audits ask whether GE answers cite verifiable sources (Liu et al., 2023; Narayanan Venkit et al., 2025; Venkit et al., 2026), user studies ask how people search with GEs (Miroyan et al., 2026; Kirsten et al., 2026), and one-off experiments show that injected page content can change the rankings a GE returns (Pfrommer et al., 2024; Nestaas et al., 2025); none of them offers a standing benchmark on which GEO strategies can be compared. Outside GEO, live benchmarks keep evaluation current by refreshing test items against contamination, as in LiveBench and LiveCodeBench (Sainz et al., 2023; White et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2025), or by continually collecting human judgments, as in Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024). LIVE-GEO brings this live design to GEO.

Numerical Faithfulness in GEO. Prior work has addressed factual errors through factual-consistency detection, such as MiniCheck (Tang et al., 2024), and verification-based revision methods, including Chain-of-Verification and RARR (Dhuliawala et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023a). Claim-verification datasets over tables and text, including TabFact, FEVEROUS, and SciTab (Chen et al., 2020; Aly et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2023), pair numerical claims with structured evidence; we draw the test cases for our verifier from them (Table 5).

Key Differences. LIVE-GEO differs from prior work in three respects. Unlike fixed-source and retrieval-pipeline benchmarks, it publishes Original and rewritten products on the live Web, so GEs retrieve and rank the pages themselves. Unlike one-off live tests, it is a standing benchmark with frozen snapshots, randomized candidate order, and recorded identity and price settings, so measurements by different users are comparable. Unlike verification methods that revise text, it flags numerical claims against product specifications (Section 3.3) without changing the text or the observed rankings.

3. LIVE-GEO Benchmark

LIVE-GEO tests whether GEO gains survive on the live Web. It publishes rewritten products as live webpages and lets GEs such as ChatGPT and Gemini rank them. Each brand has an Original product, and each submitted GEO rewrite becomes a new rewritten product of the same brand with the same specifications. We measure a product’s visibility by its position in the ranking that a GE returns for a category query such as best XX, and a strategy’s GEO gain by the visibility of its rewritten products relative to the other products of the same brand. Figure 2 shows the five stages, which the subsections below describe in turn.

3.1. Catalogue of Fictional Products

We construct fictional products and brands in 80 uncommon categories to reduce interference with existing brands and webpages. These categories span 18 product families (Appendix Table 7), with one brand per category and six predefined specification attributes per family. A Python generator uses a fixed random seed to sample specification values and insert them into predefined templates, producing an Original description and seven reviews grounded in those specifications. All products within a brand share the same non-price specifications, enabling comparisons of products that differ only in their descriptions, reviews, and a small price offset.

Users download a public raw JSON file containing category and brand information, non-price specifications, a description, and seven reviews with their identifiers, titles, text, authors, dates, and ratings. Only the description and review titles and text may be rewritten. After accepting an upload, the platform assigns the rewritten product a price drawn at random within ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% of the brand’s base price and names it by combining the brand name with the uploaded filename.

3.2. Rewriting and Submission

Users may apply any GEO strategy to the editable JSON fields and upload one file per strategy at any time, without an account, email, or invitation. After an initial submission is accepted, the platform issues a receipt token for updates under the same filename before a snapshot is frozen; new strategies require an unused filename. Submissions undergo two checks: a lightweight code gate rejects malformed or incomplete files, changes to read-only fields, and prohibited content such as HTML, scripts, links, images, or hidden characters before storage; a separate JEV safety screen identifies and rejects potentially malicious content targeting the platform, its visitors, or AI systems, and we then review each remaining file manually. Files that pass these checks proceed to numerical-faithfulness verification (Section 3.3).

3.3. Faithfulness Verification

We define numerical faithfulness as requiring concrete numerical claims in product descriptions to be consistent with and supported by the product specifications. A description violates this policy if it contradicts a specified value or introduces unsupported numerical information. Equivalent unit conversions and values directly derivable from the specifications are considered faithful. Non-numerical claims are outside the scope of this check.

After safety screening and manual review, JEV (Deußer et al., 2026) checks each submitted description against its product specifications before publication. We choose JEV because it supports fixed-choice classification with associated probabilities, fitting our policy-based verification task without generating replacement text. The same verification policy is applied across GEO strategies. This check covers rewritten descriptions only; Original descriptions and reviews are excluded.

Descriptions identified as potentially violating the numerical policy receive advisory flags. These flags do not cause rejection, text deletion, or automatic ranking changes. We export flagged products to a separate JSON file, leaving product-page content unchanged. Users who apply a ranking penalty can place flagged products after unflagged ones while preserving the relative order within each group.

3.4. Publication in Frozen Snapshots

LIVE-GEO publishes accepted submissions in frozen snapshots. Before a snapshot is frozen, users may submit new GEO strategies or revise their uploaded text at any time; once it is frozen, its content no longer changes. A snapshot fixes the candidate products, content versions, public names, prices, and page-building configuration, so a product’s rank does not shift because competitors were added or updated after the freeze. The first snapshot includes six products for each brand (one Original and five rewritten by the GEO strategies evaluated in this paper), each with a separate URL. A snapshot carries an identifier and its freeze time, which users record together with the capture time of each measurement, so that a ranking can be traced back to the exact products and text it was measured on.

3.5. Live Observation

Users evaluate published products through GEs, for example by asking for the best product in a category and requesting a ranking of the candidates. LIVE-GEO supports two query entry points: a brand-page URL, from which the GE is asked to discover and open individual products, or the product-page URLs supplied directly. To keep a fixed candidate order from favoring any product, the brand page lists its products in a new random order on every request; when supplying product URLs, we shuffle them once per brand and retain that order across repeated measurements. Users may design their own prompts. Our study uses a fixed template within each experimental condition and evaluates ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok. Appendix D provides the prompts.

4. Experiments

We examine whether the same GEO rewrites receive similar rankings across evaluators and experimental conditions. We compare rankings produced by three GEs (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok) with those of five direct-text evaluators (Table 1). We address four research questions:

RQ1: How consistent is GEO visibility across GEs and direct-text evaluators?

RQ2: How sensitive is visibility to repeated evaluation, candidate order, and public identity?

RQ3: How do small price differences and URL entry conditions affect observed visibility?

RQ4: How reliable are numerical-faithfulness flags, and how does applying them affect visibility?

4.1. Experimental Setup

Dataset. We evaluate five GEO strategies on the 80 brands. Each brand has an Original product and five rewritten products produced by Statistics Addition (Aggarwal et al., 2024), C-SEO (Puerto et al., 2025), E-GEO (Bagga et al., 2026), AgenticGEO (Yuan et al., 2026), and CORE (Jin et al., 2026); each product shows a description and seven reviews, so every ranking compares six candidates.

GEO baselines. We generate the descriptions with the methods’ released prompts or code and apply the same rewriting instructions to the review titles and bodies, keeping the specifications and the review identities, order, and ratings unchanged. The four non-CORE strategies use GPT-4.1. For CORE, we keep the authors’ ranking-feedback and suffix-optimization loop: GPT-3.5 Turbo writes the initial suffix, GPT-4o ranks candidates and optimizes later suffixes, and each suffix also guides the rewriting of the seven reviews. In a final live-feedback phase, rankings observed from ChatGPT for CORE’s non-winning products are fed back to its optimizer for further rounds. All texts are then frozen; the rankings used as optimization feedback are not counted as evaluation results.

Evaluators. We compare three GEs (ChatGPT with GPT-6, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, and Grok in Expert mode) with five direct-text evaluators (four APIs: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.6, and Claude Sonnet 5.5; one local model: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025)). The GEs receive the published product URLs or a brand URL and rank the six products after reading the pages. The direct-text evaluators receive the frozen descriptions and reviews as text, without web access. The Claude API returned complete rankings for 78 of the 80 brands and refused the remaining two requests, possibly because their content triggered Anthropic’s usage policy (Anthropic, 2026); Claude results therefore use n=78n=78.

Experimental conditions. We design experiments on the URL entry point (product URLs or a brand URL), candidate order, public identity, and price, while the product records stay fixed. In the product-URL condition, we shuffle each brand’s six links once locally and keep that order for repeated measurements; in the brand-URL condition, the GE opens the brand page, whose product order the site randomizes on each request. For order sensitivity, we use two fixed product-URL sequences on ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok under equal prices, ordered by the strategies’ mean ranks in the initial ChatGPT equal-price run (Table 1): Original-first (Original, AgenticGEO, C-SEO, Statistics Addition, E-GEO, CORE) and its exact reverse. For identity sensitivity, we replace all six strategy names, including Original, with neutral aliases assigned at random within each brand and applied to page text, URLs, and navigation (Appendix C). For price sensitivity, we compare equal prices with prices frozen within ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% of each brand’s base price.

Protocol and metrics. All GE conditions use one ranking prompt adapted from CORE (Jin et al., 2026), with small changes for webpage access and output format (Figure 3; full prompts in Appendix D). The prompt asks the evaluator to open the six product pages, read the descriptions and displayed reviews, and return a complete ranking with a reading record per product. For each request we keep the content snapshot, URLs, prompt, capture time, model-setting evidence, raw response, and parsed ranking; only complete permutations of the six candidates enter the statistics. We measure each strategy’s overall performance by its Top-1 rate and mean rank. To compare two conditions, we compute Spearman’s ρ\rho between the two rankings within each brand and average it across brands, and we report the share of brands with the same top product and the same last product, and the mean absolute rank difference. Uncertainty in paired comparisons is given as a 95% bootstrap interval from 10,000 brand resamples (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993). Missing or incomplete rankings are excluded from the denominator.

4.2. Evaluation

We first compare rankings across evaluators (RQ1), then examine their sensitivity to repeated evaluation, candidate order, public identity, and prices (RQ2–RQ3). Finally, we report numerical-faithfulness flags and examine how placing flagged products below unflagged ones changes the recorded rankings (RQ4). Each question asks whether a visibility gain measured under one condition survives on the live Web.

Ranking consistency across evaluators (RQ1). Under frozen ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices, CORE leads Top-1 rates across seven evaluators (Table 1). On the three GEs, CORE’s Top-1 rate is 76.3% (ChatGPT), 67.5% (Grok), and 66.3% (Gemini), with mean ranks of 1.74, 2.21, and 2.01 and margins of 56 to 66 percentage points over the second-best strategy. The exception is the Claude API, which ranks Original first (44.9%) and E-GEO second (41.0%), while CORE comes last with a mean rank of 5.56. Qwen also ranks CORE first, but with a Top-1 rate of 23.8% and a spread of 1.49 it barely separates the strategies.

Agreement in the aggregate does not imply agreement on individual brands (Table 3). Each pair of GEs selects the same top product for only 48.8% to 66.3% of brands, with mean ρ\rho between 0.32 and 0.48; for the active-layer thaw-bed planter, for example, Grok selects Statistics Addition and Gemini selects CORE. The direct-text evaluators differ widely in how closely they follow the GEs (Figure 4): DeepSeek reaches ρ=0.50\rho=0.50 and the same top product as ChatGPT on 66.3% of brands, matching the agreement among the GEs themselves; GPT-4o and Kimi are intermediate (ρ\rho from 0.25 to 0.41); Qwen is weak (ρ≤0.20\rho\leq 0.20); and Claude correlates negatively with all three GEs (ρ\rho from −0.31-0.31 to −0.22-0.22, same top product below 10%). Agreement on the last product is similarly limited, ranging from 7.7% (Claude and Gemini) to 68.8% (DeepSeek and Grok), and it exceeds agreement on the top product in only half of the pairs.

Repeatability and presentation sensitivity (RQ2). Repeating the ChatGPT evaluation with the same text, prompt, and product-URL order gives stable aggregate results: the two runs select the same top product for 80.0% of brands and the same last product for 90.0%, with mean ρ=0.85\rho=0.85, and CORE’s Top-1 rate is 82.5% and 83.8% (Tables 1 and 3); no strategy’s mean-rank change between the two runs has an interval that excludes zero (Table 2).

Candidate order changes the observed ranking. On ChatGPT, CORE’s Top-1 rate under the two fixed orders is 73.8% (Original-first) and 93.8% (reverse), a difference of 20 percentage points, and its margin grows from 60.0 to 90.0 (Table 1). In the paired contrasts (Table 2), the reverse order improves CORE’s mean rank by 0.79 and worsens C-SEO’s and Statistics Addition’s by 0.29 and 0.48, all with intervals excluding zero. On Grok, the same two sequences give CORE Top-1 rates of 37.5% and 50.0%; on Gemini, the highest Top-1 rate moves from E-GEO (30.0%) under Original-first to CORE (28.8%) under the reverse order (Table 1). ChatGPT’s random-order results fall between its two fixed orders, which is why LIVE-GEO randomizes the candidate order for each brand and keeps that order for repeated measurements. The direct-text APIs are also order-sensitive (Table 4): after reversing the saved order, ρ\rho is 0.33 to 0.37 for DeepSeek, 0.39 to 0.49 for Kimi, and 0.76 to 0.85 for Claude, with the same top product on 43.6% to 72.5% of brands.

Compared with the unmasked repeat, the masked run (Appendix C) gives CORE a lower Top-1 rate (76.3% versus 83.8%) and Statistics Addition a higher rate (21.3% versus 12.5%) (Table 1); Statistics Addition’s mean rank improves by 0.60 with an interval excluding zero (Table 2). The masked and unmasked runs select the same top product for 78.8% of brands, with ρ=0.79\rho=0.79 (Table 3).

Price and URL entry conditions (RQ3). With product URLs, the leading strategy stays the same between equal and frozen ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices, while the values change (Table 1). With product URLs, CORE’s Top-1 rate moves from 82.5% to 76.3% on ChatGPT, from 65.0% to 67.5% on Grok, and from 82.5% to 66.3% on Gemini, and it remains first on all three GEs. In the paired comparison (Table 2), only four intervals exclude zero: on ChatGPT, Original’s mean rank improves by 0.59 and E-GEO’s worsens by 0.54; on Gemini, CORE’s worsens by 0.63 and AgenticGEO’s improves by 0.33.

Rankings also differ across URL-entry conditions. With ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices, CORE’s Top-1 rate on Grok is 71.3% with the brand URL and 67.5% with product URLs, with mean ranks of 2.04 and 2.21; on ChatGPT the values are 46.3% and 76.3%, with mean ranks of 2.45 and 1.74 (Table 1).

Numerical-faithfulness flags (RQ4). JEV flags 86 of the 400 rewritten descriptions (Table 1, last row): all 80 Statistics Addition descriptions, 3 from AgenticGEO, 2 from E-GEO, 1 from CORE, and none from C-SEO. The Statistics Addition prompt asks for compelling statistics and permits hypothetical data, so numbers unsupported by the specifications are common, for example an “18% improvement in heat retention”; flagged descriptions from other strategies also contain unsupported comparisons, such as CORE’s “30% energy savings” and AgenticGEO’s “up to 60% less water use.”

To test the verifier, we apply it to 194 numerical test cases drawn from SciTab, TabFact, and FEVEROUS, where JEV agrees with the reference labels on 176 cases (90.72%; Table 5). We also validate it against human reviewers: three researchers independently reviewed 50 randomly sampled descriptions (ten per strategy) without seeing JEV’s output. JEV agrees with the two-of-three majority on all 50 descriptions, 49 of which are unanimous, and Fleiss’ κ\kappa is 0.96 (Table 6); all ten majority flags belong to Statistics Addition.

We place flagged products after unflagged ones and keep the Original order within each group, which gives the flag-adjusted rows in Table 1. After the adjustment, Statistics Addition has a Top-1 rate of zero in every condition and a mean rank of 5.95 to 5.96; under the ChatGPT product-URL condition, CORE’s Top-1 rate rises from 82.5% to 86.3% and E-GEO’s from 10.0% to 13.8%.

4.3. Results and Discussion

Do GEO gains survive the live Web? Some gains survive and others do not. On the same frozen text and under the randomized candidate order, four direct-text evaluators (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Kimi, and Qwen) and all three GEs give CORE the highest Top-1 rate, and this Top-1 lead holds under both price settings and both entry points on ChatGPT and Grok (RQ1, RQ3). Two things do not carry over. The ordering measured under Claude reverses on the GEs, and agreement in the aggregate does not extend to brands: the GEs pick different winners for a third to a half of the brands, the brand-level agreement between direct-text evaluators and GEs is lower still, and only DeepSeek approaches the level seen among the GEs. Part of the aggregate gain therefore survives, whereas much of the brand-level gain does not.

LIVE-GEO as a benchmark. The experiments above also test LIVE-GEO itself. It is a public, Kaggle-style platform: fictional products for 80 brands are published on the live Web; users download the original descriptions and reviews, rewrite them with their own method, and upload the result; and each submission becomes a rewritten product of that brand, ranked by GEs under the category query together with the Original and the earlier submissions. Every control used in the experiments is a fixed design of the platform: content snapshots are frozen, so repeated measurements can be reproduced; the candidate order is drawn at random per brand and kept across repeats, so order effects are measured rather than hidden; the public strategy labels are a known treatment factor; prices are perturbed within a fixed band; and JEV flags with human review stop submissions that trade unsupported numbers for rank. The three GEs returned complete rankings for all 80 brands under product URLs, which shows that the benchmark is feasible. Users choose the GEs that can reach the site and their own prompts, run the measurements, and report them themselves; because everyone faces the same frozen set of control products, numbers from different users are comparable. The more submissions arrive, the larger the set of strategies each new submission competes against.

5. Conclusion

We present LIVE-GEO, a benchmark that publishes GEO-rewritten products on the live Web and lets GEs rank them under their own retrieval conditions; it freezes content snapshots and records the candidate order, public identity, and price setting, so that visibility measurements from different users are comparable. An evaluation on 80 brands, five strategies, and eight evaluators answers the question in the title: part of the aggregate GEO gain survives on the live Web, but most brand-level gains do not, and LIVE-GEO narrows this gap by letting users measure their own gains where GEs read the pages.

Appendix A Evaluated Product Families

Table 7 lists the 18 product families of the 80-brand cohort and the number of brands in each.

Appendix B Additional Results

Figure 4 extends Table 3 to all 28 evaluator pairs: the highest agreement among direct-text evaluators is between GPT-4o and DeepSeek (ρ=0.62\rho=0.62), above any pair that involves a GE, and Claude correlates negatively with every other evaluator. Figure 5 breaks the Top-1 rates of Table 1 down by product family for the three GEs under frozen ±0.2%\pm 0.2\% prices; families are ordered by CORE’s share on ChatGPT. Table 8 lists the top-ranked product of every brand for the three GEs and DeepSeek.

Appendix C Identity Masking

In the masked condition, each brand’s six strategy labels, including Original, are replaced by six neutral aliases (Luma, Tavi, Neri, Vela, Sori, and Miro), shuffled independently within each brand with a fixed seed; a product named Brand CORE, for example, becomes Brand Vela. The alias replaces the full product name and any standalone strategy label in titles, page metadata, links, descriptions, and reviews, while all other wording, the specifications, and the prices stay unchanged. Masked pages use opaque URL paths, navigation to unmasked pages is disabled, and the alias-to-strategy mapping is kept private.

Appendix D Ranking Prompts

We adapt CORE’s ranking prompt with small adjustments for LIVE-GEO’s webpage evaluation setting. The product-URL template below reproduces the saved protocol with category and URL placeholders. The six URLs follow the frozen per-brand order. Opposite-order conditions change only their sequence; the masked condition substitutes the mapped URLs. Brand-URL requests replace the six-page introduction with “Use the following brand page to discover its six candidate products:” and supply one URL. The price requests additionally require a displayed_price field in each reading-log entry. Neither prompt supplies previous ranks.

You are a helpful assistant. The user query is:
best {category}
Use the following six candidate product pages:
<listing URL 1>
…
<listing URL 6>
Before ranking, open each individual product page and read its product description and all displayed customer comments. Do not judge from the brand-page summaries alone.
After reading, recommend the products by producing a ranked list from most to least relevant to the user query. Only use the information provided on these pages.
Return a JSON object containing:
1. “ranking”: an array of the six exact product names, ordered from rank 1 (best) to rank 6 (worst).
2. “reading_log”: one entry per product, containing:
“product_name”; “product_url”; “description_read”: “full”, “partial”, or “none”; “comments_displayed”: the number of individual comments exposed by the page, or null if unknown; “comments_read”: the number actually read, or null if unknown; “access_limitation”: a brief description of any missing or inaccessible content, or null.
The aggregate review count is not the number of comments displayed. Do not treat it as the number read.
Report access and reading coverage honestly. Do not invent content, counts, or reading percentages.
Include a “limitations” field:
Use null if all six descriptions and all individually displayed comments were fully read. Otherwise, describe only the actual access gaps in one sentence of at most 40 words. A larger aggregate review count than the displayed comment count is not an access failure. Do not include ranking explanations or general disclaimers in this field.

The direct-text evaluators receive one user message built from the same frozen records, with the six products as a JSON array:

You are a helpful assistant. The user query is: best {category}
The candidate products are:
[one object per product with “name”, “price”, “rating”, and “description” (the product description followed by the seven customer comments)]
Recommend the products by producing a ranked list from most to least relevant to the user query.
Only use the provided information in the JSON input.
Return ONLY a JSON array of product names in ranked order, from rank 1 (best) to rank N (worst).
Example format: [“Product A”, “Product B”, “Product C”]
